plain_text:
Despite progress since the Paris Agreement, per capita emissions in several OECD countries remain
above the global average. While countries like the United Kingdom have successfully reduced their per
capita emissions below this threshold (5.4 tCO2e), others - such as Australia and Canada - still emit
approximately three times more per person. This disparity is tied to income levels, with high-emitting
households concentrated in wealthier nations (UNEP, 2024 [2] ). Meanwhile, per capita emissions in
emerging economies like China and Brazil have risen, driven by rapid economic growth (Figure 1.13 ).
However, some of the observed reductions in territorial per capita emissions may be due to the outsourcing
of carbon-intensive production (Figure 1.14 ).
